analysis.one_liner: Requires 'made with AI' labels on political ads and extends ad disclosure rules to large online platforms.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan-idea bill with three Democratic sponsors to require AI-content labels on political ads was introduced in May 2023 and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require any political advertisement that contains an AI-generated image or video to carry a clear, plainly visible label saying so, with specific rules for text, audio, and video ads. It would also close a long-standing gap by requiring campaigns to report paid internet and digital political ads to the Federal Election Commission, the same way TV and radio ads already are, and would apply these rules to large online platforms and ad networks. The FEC would write detailed regulations defining what counts as AI-generated content.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would know when the images and videos in political ads were fabricated by AI rather than filmed, and could judge ads accordingly. Candidates and groups that play by the rules would also benefit from uniform, enforceable disclosure standards that are hard for dishonest competitors to evade.

how_it_helps.text: Requires any political ad containing an AI-generated image or video to state that clearly, with the label appearing in type as large as most of the ad's text, spoken for at least three seconds in audio ads, or both on screen for four seconds and audible in video ads.
Closes a disclosure gap by treating paid internet and digital political ads on large platforms like TV and radio ads, which must already be reported to the Federal Election Commission.

Directs the FEC to write regulations defining what counts as AI-generated content and how to judge whether an ad contains it, covering current and future AI uses that carry a high risk of spreading misinformation about candidates and elections.

analysis.who_pays: Large online platforms (social networks, search engines, and big ad networks with 50 million or more monthly U.S. users) and the political ad industry would bear new compliance duties: applying disclaimers, reporting paid digital ads to the FEC, and monitoring AI-generated content in ads they sell. Campaigns and outside groups would bear the cost of labeling their AI-generated ad content.

drawbacks.text: The rules would fall on large platforms and ad vendors, which would have to police AI-generated content in ads they host and report paid digital ads to the FEC — a compliance burden that platforms and advertisers were likely to fight in rulemaking and court.

A disclaimer only tells viewers that AI was used somewhere in an ad; it does not prevent deepfaked images or fabricated events from appearing in political ads at all, so the bill informs rather than restricts.

The disclosure requirement applies to communications covered by the existing ad-disclaimer rules, and defining what counts as 'generated in whole or in part' with AI is technically difficult — lightly edited real footage or minor AI touch-ups could be hard to classify, which the FEC would have to untangle in regulation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: a label on AI-fabricated imagery gives voters a fact they can act on, and extending ad-reporting rules to digital platforms closes a loophole that has existed since campaigns moved online. The costs are compliance burdens concentrated on a handful of giant platforms and some friction for advertisers, which seems proportionate. The main weakness is that the bill labels AI content rather than barring the most deceptive uses, so it mitigates rather than solves the deepfake problem in elections.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Rules Committee from the day it was introduced and never got a markup, a committee vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on May 15, 2023, joined by Senators Booker and Bennet.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Rules and Administration the same day; that referral was the last action of any kind in the bill's record.
No committee vote, hearing, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large digital ad platforms and political advertisers are better off, since they face no federal AI-labeling or digital ad-reporting requirements from this bill. Voters are left with no mandatory disclosure of AI-fabricated imagery in political ads.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.role: Senate Rules and Administration Chair; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited three cosponsors, but her own committee never scheduled it for action.

for.name: Sens. Cory Booker and Michael Bennet

against.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only three Democratic senators sponsored the bill and no Republican cosponsor joined, but no one ever voted on it, so the actual partisan split never got tested.

industries.industry: Large online ad platforms and ad networks
industries.note: The bill would subject social networks, search engines, and big ad vendors selling political ads to disclaimer, reporting, and AI-content-monitoring rules, and would pull paid digital ads into FEC electioneering-communication rules for the first time. Platforms profiting from political ad sales with less scrutiny have an interest in keeping that scrutiny off, which runs against voters' interest in knowing who paid for what they see.

industries.industry: Political advertising and campaign consulting firms
industries.note: Ad makers and media buyers would have to label AI-generated imagery and fit digital buys into FEC reporting rules, adding cost and legal exposure. The rules would apply evenly, so compliant firms would not be disadvantaged against honest competitors.

The bill regulates the use of AI output in political ads, not the tools themselves, so providers face no direct restrictions; their models would simply carry a labeling duty when used in political advertising.
